newsitem.title: UK: Broker cuts nickel outlook, sees dip in stainless.
newsitem.headline: Broker cuts nickel outlook, sees dip in stainless.

text.p: Less demand from the stainless steel industry and greater availability of scrap will lead to a more balanced nickel market than expected this year, broker Brandeis said in a report.
The market will also see a rise in mine production and steady exports from Russia and Cuba, it added.
The view of a more balanced market prompted Brandeis to trim its view of average three month nickel prices on the London Metal Exchange (LME) this year to $8,117 per tonne from $8,598.
Prices should climb to an average of $8,762 next year, the broker added. On Thursday morning LME prices were flucuating between $7,150 and $7,200.
The Western world refined nickel market is expected to be largely in balance in 1997, with a deficit of 4,000 tonnes after a surplus of the same amount last year, Brandeis said.
"We believe that in the second half of 1997, there may be a need for stainless steel production cuts in the Western world, particularly in southeast Asia," the report said.
Some destocking of stainless steel inventories appears to have taken place in the United States, Germany and South Korea, but overall inventories are still historically high.
"We believe that the amount of true destocking in 1996 has been overestimated and that stocks remain relatively high," Brandeis said.
Stainless steel mills were reluctant to cut output last year in an effort to keep costs to a minium by producing at capacity.

At the same time, the availability of scrap remains better than expected, with supplies being shipped from Russia to Europe and the U.S. Some analysts had expected a shortage of scrap would increase the demand for primary metal this year.
"In our opinion, the scrap tightness story has been overdone and mills are still trying to maximise their margins by using as much scrap as well as ferronickel as they can."
Refined nickel output should increase by 4.7 percent in 1997, following the completion of several expansion and upgrading programmes at existing plants.
Russian exports are seen dipping in 1997 and 1998 but shipments from Cuba are expected to rise, resulting in a slight decline in East Bloc exports of 2,000 tonnes to 168,000 tonnes this year.
